title: The Fragmented Page
text:
Postmodern fiction often refuses the comfort of a single, reliable narrator. Instead, authors scatter their stories across fragmented chapters, footnotes, and contradictory testimonies, leaving the reader to assemble a coherent meaning. Critics have argued that this technique reflects a broader scepticism toward grand explanations of history and identity. Whether such fragmentation liberates the reader or merely exhausts them remains a matter of fierce debate.

Some experimental novelists go further by inserting blank pages, typographical irregularities, or diagrams that interrupt the flow of the narrative. These devices are not decorative; they force the reader to notice the act of reading itself. Consequently, the text becomes less a window onto a fictional world than an object that draws attention to its own construction. Many readers find this unsettling, yet it has inspired a loyal following among those who value formal daring.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what do postmodern authors often refuse to provide?

options: They are included mainly to decorate the book

questions.text: What does the passage suggest about readers who value formal daring?
options: They generally prefer traditional narratives with clear endings
They are indifferent to the way a book is constructed
They are likely to appreciate texts that draw attention to their own construction
They believe fragmentation is merely exhausting

paragraph_translations: Postmodern fiction often avoids giving readers a single, dependable narrator. Instead, authors spread their stories across broken chapters, footnotes, and conflicting statements, so the reader has to build a consistent meaning. Critics have argued that this method reflects a wider doubt about large explanations of history and identity. Whether such fragmentation frees the reader or simply wears them out is still strongly debated.

Some experimental novelists go further by putting blank pages, irregular printing, or diagrams into the text, which interrupt the flow of the story. These features are not decorative; they make the reader notice the act of reading itself. As a result, the text becomes less a window onto an imagined world and more an object that draws attention to how it was made. Many readers find this disturbing, yet it has won a devoted audience among those who value bold experiments in form.
